text: Richard Serra (November 2, 1938 – March 26, 2024) was an American artist renowned for his large-scale abstract sculptures installed in site-specific landscape, urban, and architectural environments, and is primarily associated with postminimalism. Described as "one of his era's greatest sculptors," Serra emphasized the material qualities of his works and explored the relationship between the viewer, the artwork, and its site. Born in San Francisco on November 2, 1938, to Tony and Gladys Serra—second of three sons—the son of a Spanish father from Mallorca and a mother, Gladys (née Fineberg), daughter of Russian Jewish immigrants from Odessa, USSR—was encouraged to draw by his mother, who introduced him as "Richard the artist." His father worked as a pipe fitter at a shipyard near San Francisco, and Serra recalled a memory of watching a boat launch at age four, noting, "All the raw material that I needed is contained in the reserve of this memory." His father, related to the Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí, later worked as a candy plant foreman. Serra studied English literature at the University of California, Berkeley in 1957 before transferring to the University of California, Santa Barbara, where he graduated in 1961 with a B.A. in English Literature, meeting muralists Rico Lebrun and Howard Warshaw. To support himself, he worked in steel mills from ages 16 to 25. He then attended Yale University, earning a B.A. in art history and an M.F.A. in 1964. During a one-year traveling fellowship in Paris in 1964, he met composer Philip Glass, who became a collaborator and long-time friend, and visited Constantin Brâncuși's studio, partially reconstructed at the Musée national d'Art moderne on the Avenue du Président Wilson, which influenced his sculptural approach. Serra spent 1965 in Florence, Italy on a Fulbright Grant and visited the Prado Museum in Madrid in 1966, where he saw Diego Velázquez's painting *Las Meninas* and decided to move away from painting. In Europe, he began experimenting with nontraditional materials, exhibiting "Animal Habitats" at Galleria Salita in Rome, which referenced early Arte Povera works. Returning to the United States in 1966, he continued using experimental materials such as rubber, neon, latex, fiberglass, and lead. His Belt Pieces used gravity to form rubber strips hung on walls, and he created *Belts (1966–67)* by combining neon with rubber, referencing Jackson Pollock's *Mural (1963)*. He wrote *Verb List (1967)*, a list of transitive verbs like "cast," "roll," "tear," and "prop," which guided his sculptures. Works such as *To Lift (1967)*, where a 10-foot sheet of rubber was lifted into a free-standing form, and *Thirty-Five Feet of Lead Rolled Up (1968)*, created with the help of Philip Glass, reflected his interest in industrial materials and physical properties. In 1968, he exhibited *Prop (1968)*, *Scatter Piece (1968)*, and *Splashing (1968)* at the Castelli Warehouse in New York, where molten lead was thrown against walls and floors. In 1969, *Casting* was included in the Whitney Museum's *Anti-Illusion: Procedures/Materials* exhibition, where molten lead was splashed and pulled away from walls to create free-standing forms. The verb "to prop" led to a series of lead plate and pole assemblages, with *One Ton Prop: House of Cards (1969)*—a self-supporting structure of four lead plates weighing one ton—marking a move away from wall dependency. In 1969, while working with Jasper Johns, Serra created *Strike: To Roberta and Rudy (1969–71)*, a steel plate wedged into a corner that divided a room into two equal spaces, altering the viewer's perception as they moved around it. In 1969, during the "Art and Technology" exhibition at LACMA, Serra developed the Skullcracker Series, building ephemeral steel stacks up to 30 to 40 feet (9 to 12 meters) high and weighing 60 to 70 tons (54.4 to 63.5 tons), which were knocked down daily by steelworkers, marking a shift toward large-scale works beyond gallery settings. In 1970, Serra received a Guggenheim Fellowship and traveled to Japan, where he created his first outdoor sculptures, *To Encircle Base Plate (Hexagram) (1970)* and *Sugi Tree (1970)*, installed in Ueno Park, Tokyo as part of the Tokyo Biennale. While in Kyoto, he studied Zen gardens and temples at Myoshin-ji, which influenced his perception of space in relation to time. Upon returning, he created *To Encircle Base Plate Hexagram, Right Angles Inverted (1970)*, embedding two semi-circular steel flanges—1 inch and 8 inches wide—into 183rd Street in the Bronx, visible from two perspectives. Throughout the 1970s, Serra produced outdoor site-specific works exploring landscape topography and viewer movement. His first landscape work, *Pulitzer Piece: Stepped Elevation (1970–71)*, was commissioned by Joseph and Emily Rauh Pulitzer for their property outside St. Louis, Missouri, consisting of three plates 5 feet high by 40 to 50 feet long placed across approximately 3 acres, impaled into the ground so their rise was 5 feet, acting as surrogate horizons. *Shift (1970–1972)*, built in King City, Ontario, consisted of six rectilinear concrete sections along a sloping field, with the top edges forming a horizon at specific elevational intervals; it was designated a Heritage Site in 2013. Notable landscape works include *Porten i Slugten (1983–1986)* at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Humlebaek, Denmark, where two angled plates at the end of a path form a gate-like structure that appears to swing as viewers walk toward the sea; *Carnegie (1985)* outside the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh; *Afangar (Stations, Stops on the Road, To Stop and Look: Forward and Back, To Take It All In) (1990)* on Videy Island, Iceland, consisting of nine pairs of basalt columns placed at elevations of 9 and 10 meters, with stones measuring 3 meters at higher and 4 meters at lower levels, varying in spacing due to topography; *Schunnemunk Fork (1991)* in Storm King Art Center, New York; *Snake Eyes and Box Cars (1993)* in Sonoma County, California; *Te Tuhirangi Contour (2000–2002)* in Kaipara, New Zealand, a 20-foot-high, 844-foot-long contour following the rolling hills; and *East-West/West-East (2014)* in Qatar, consisting of four steel plates—543⁄4 or 481⁄2 feet high—placed at irregular intervals in a valley between two gypsum plateaus, all level with each other and the adjacent plateaus, visible from either end. In urban settings, Serra's site-specific works, such as *Sight Point (1972–1975)* at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam, *Terminal (1977)* in Bochum, Germany, *T.W.U. (1980)* at Deichtorhallen in Hamburg, *Fulcrum (1986–87)* in Broadgate, London, *Exchange (1996)* outside Luxembourg, and *7 (2011)* on a pier in Doha, Qatar, reflect verticality and balance, often inviting viewers to walk through or around them. Curved works like *St. John's Rotary Arc (1980)*, temporarily installed at the Holland Tunnel entrance in New York City; *Tilted Arc (1981)*, installed and later removed from Federal Plaza in New York City; *Clara-Clara (1983)* at Tuileries, Place de la Concorde, Paris; and *Berlin Junction (1987)* outside the Berlin Philharmonic, open and close depending on the viewer's direction of movement. Serra was married to artist Nancy Graves from 1965 to 1970 and to Clara Weyergraf from 1981 until his death in 2024.

Deichtorhallen in Hamburg, Germany; Fulcrum (1986–87), installed in Broadgate, London; Exchange (1996) outside the City of Luxembourg; or 7 (2011) on a pier in Doha, Qatar, reflect the verticality of their surrounding architecture. Outdoor sculptures such as St. John's Rotary Arc (1980), temporarily installed outside the Holland Tunnel entrance in New York City; Tilted Arc (1981), installed and later removed from New York City's Federal Plaza; Clara-Clara (1983), temporarily installed at Tuileries, Place de la Concorde, Paris; and Berlin Junction (1987), installed outside the Berlin Philharmonic, are all curved forms or arcs that open and close depending on the direction the viewer takes while walking around them. Sight Point (1972–1975) was Serra's first vertical Urban work and a continuation of the balance and counterbalance principles of his earlier work Prop. It stands outside the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam, the Netherlands, consisting of three vertical steel plates 10 feet (3 m) wide and 40 feet (12 m) high that lean in at an angle, forming a triangular space on the ground with three openings that can be walked through; once inside, the viewer can look up and see the sky framed by the triangular shape made by the leaning plates. Another vertical sculpture, Terminal (1977), was conceived for "Documenta VI" in 1977 and permanently installed on a traffic island between street car tracks in front of a train station in Bochum, Germany. Serra chose the site due to its proximity to a high-traffic area. Exchange (1996), sited in a vehicular round-about on top of a highway tunnel, is made of seven trapezoidal plates and stands 60 feet (18 m) high, visible to drivers entering and leaving the City of Luxembourg. In 1980, Serra installed two sculptures with the support of the Public Art Fund in New York City: T.W.U. (1980), a vertical sculpture consisting of three vertical plates each 36 feet (11 m) high, installed at a subway entrance near West Broadway between Leonard and Franklin Streets, is now permanently installed outside the Deichtorhallen, Hamburg, Germany; and St. John's Rotary Arc (1980), one of Serra's earliest curved sculptures, 12 feet (3.6 m) high and spanning 180 feet (55 m), was installed from 1980 to 1988 on the rotary at the entrance and exit to the Holland Tunnel. In 1981, Tilted Arc (1981) was installed in New York City's Federal Plaza, commissioned by the U.S. General Services Administration's Art-in-Architecture Program after a rigorous selection process; the sculpture's arc spanned 120 feet (36 m) and was 12 feet (3.6 m) high, tilting and leaning away from its base, anchored at both ends with the center raised. Serra intended the sculpture to draw pedestrians' attention as they crossed the plaza. It faced resistance from Federal building workers, leading to an eight-year campaign to remove it, which concluded with its removal on March 15, 1989. In defense of the sculpture, Serra stated, "To remove Tilted Arc, therefore, is to destroy it," advocating an art-for-art's-sake approach to site-specific artworks. Following the hearing and GSA's decision, Serra responded that he would deny authorship of Tilted Arc if it were relocated and would consider it a "derivative work." The case of Tilted Arc continues to highlight tensions surrounding public art and its intended audience. Serra's work has been featured in numerous gallery and museum exhibitions, with his site-specific gallery installations sometimes used to test ideas. His first U.S. solo exhibition was at the Leo Castelli Warehouse, New York City in 1969, where he exhibited ten lead Prop Pieces, a Scatter Piece: Cutting Device: Base Plate Measure (1969), and a Splash Piece: Splashing with Four Molds (To Eva Hesse) (1969). After his process-based works of the late 1960s and early 1970s, Serra began to solely use rolled or forged steel in his sculptures. Berlin Block (for Charlie Chaplin) (1977) was his first forged sculpture, made for the plaza outside the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and weighing 70 tons. Other forged sculptures include Elevation for Mies (1985–88) at Museum Haus Esters, Krefeld, Germany; Philibert et Marguerite (1985) in the Musee de Brou, Bourg-en-Bresse, France; Weight and Measure (1992), a temporary site-specific installation at the Tate Gallery, London; Santa Fe Depot (2004) in the Museum of Contemporary Art San Diego; and Equal (2015) in the Museum of Modern Art, New York. Serra's most known series of sculptures using rolled steel plates are the Torqued Ellipses. In 1991, after visiting Borromini's Church of San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane in Rome and mistaking the ovals of the dome and floor as offset, he conceived a torqued form. He created models in his studio by cutting two ellipse-shaped pieces of wood and nailing a dowel between them, then turning the ellipses at a right angle and wrapping a sheet of lead around the form. After making a template, he worked with an engineer to fabricate the sculptures. There are seven Torqued Ellipses and four Double Torqued Ellipses (an ellipse inside an ellipse) dated between 1996 and 2004. Each sculpture has a different degree of torque and measures up to 13 feet (3.9 m) high, with an opening for walking through and around. Three Torqued Ellipses are on permanent view at Dia Beacon, New York. In 2005, "The Matter of Time," a commissioned installation at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain, opened, consisting of eight sculptures spanning from 1994 to 2005 and highlighting the evolution of Serra's forms. It includes five sculptures derived from the initial torqued ellipse: one single, one double ellipse, and three torqued spirals. The Torqued Spirals followed the Double Torqued Ellipses when Serra connected a double ellipse into a single wound form that can be entered and walked through. The remaining sculptures are one closed (Blind Spot Reversed) and one open (Between the Torus and the Sphere) torus and spherical sculpture; and Snake, made of three parts, each comprising two identical conical sections inverted relative to each other and spanning 104 feet (31.7 m) overall. The sculptures are organized with intention, creating a sensation of varying scale and proportion and an awareness of the passage of time as the viewer moves through the space. In 2008, Serra participated in Monumenta at Paris's Grand Palais, installing Promenade (2008), consisting of five plates, each 55 feet (16.8 m) tall and 13 feet (4 m) wide, placed 100 feet (30 m) apart across the interior, not in a line but side by side off the center axis, tilting left or right and leaning toward or away from each other and the viewer as they stroll around them. Equal (2015), in the collection of The Museum of Modern Art, New York, consists of eight forged blocks, each measuring 5 by 5 1/2 by 6 feet (1.5 × 1.7 × 1.8 m) and weighing 40 tons, stacked in pairs and positioned on their longer or shorter sides so each stack measures 11 feet (3.4 m) tall; walking among the four stacks makes the viewer aware of their own sense of weight, balance, and gravity in relation to the sculptures. Four Rounds: Equal Weight, Unequal Measure (2017), consisting of four 82-ton (74 t) forged cylinders of varying dimensions, is permanently installed at Glenstone in Potomac, Maryland, within a building designed by Thomas Phifer of Thomas Phifer and Partners, in collaboration with Serra to highlight the sculpture's mass within the building's interior. Drawing was integral to Serra's practice; he made drawings on large sheets of canvas or handmade paper, including horizontal or vertical compositions, overlapping sheets, or line drawings, primarily in paintstick, lithographic crayon, or charcoal, always black, experimenting with techniques to create a tactile, phenomenological experience of movement, time, and space. He stated that his drawing practice involves "repetition, knowing there's no possibility of repeating, knowing that it's going to yield something different each time." After his break into space with sculptures like Strike: To Roberta and Rudy (1969–1971), Serra became interested in redefining architectural space through drawing. In 1974, he began making Installation Drawings—large-scale site-specific sheets of canvas completely covered in paintstick and stapled to the wall. Shafrazi and Zadikians were two of his first Installation Drawings, exhibited at Leo Castelli Gallery, New York City in 1974, measuring approximately 10 1/2 feet (3.2 m) high and 18 feet (5.5 m) wide. He continued making Installation Drawings throughout his career, with notable series including Diptychs (1989); Dead Weight (1991–92); Weight and Measure (1993–94); Videy Afangar (1989–1991); Rounds (1996–97); out-of-rounds (1999–2000); Line Drawings (2000–2002); Solids (2008); Greenpoint Rounds (2009); Elevational Weights (2010); Rifts (2011–2018); Transparencies (2011–2013); Horizontal Reversals (2014); Rambles (2015–16); Composites (2016); Horizontals and Verticals (2016–17); and Orchard Street (2018). National and international survey exhibitions of Serra's drawings include Richard Serra: Tekeningen/Drawings 1971–1977 at the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam in 1978; Richard Serra: Tekeningen/Drawings at the Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht in 1990; Richard Serra Drawing: A Retrospective at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and Menil Collection, Houston from 2011 to 2012; and Richard Serra: Drawings 2015–2017: Rambles, Composites, Rotterdam Verticals, Rotterdam Horizontals, Rifts at the Museum Boijmans van Beuningen, Rotterdam, The Netherlands in 2017. Serra began making prints in 1972, working closely with Gemini G.E.L. in Los Angeles, developing unconventional techniques and producing over 200 printed works that reflect an interest in process, scale, and material experimentation. His early lithographs from 1972 include Circuit; Balance; Eight by Eight; or 183rd & Webster Avenue, each titled after a sculpture created around the same time. In 1981, he produced his first lithograph series, Sketch #1 through Sketch #7, and began making larger-scale prints such as Malcolm X; Goslar, or The Moral Majority Sucks. After pushing lithography to its limit, Serra began working with silkscreen, applying a layer of ink to paper and then a layer of paintstick through a second screen to create a saturated and textured surface. He continued using this technique, sometimes combining it with etching and aquatint, with print series including Videy Afanger (1991); Hreppholer (1991); WM (1996); Rounds (1999); Venice Notebook (2001); Between the Torus and the Sphere (2006); Paths and Edges (2007); Level (2008); Junction (2010); Reversal (2015); Elevational Weight (2016); Equal (2018); and (?) (2019). From 1968 to 1979, Serra made a collection of films and videos, recognizing the different material capacities of each medium and not extending sculptural problems into his films and videos. He collaborated with artists including Joan Jonas, Nancy Holt, and Robert Fiore. His first films, Hand Catching Lead (1968), Hands Scraping (1968), and Hand Tied (1968), involve actions such as a hand trying to catch falling lead, pairs of hands moving lead shavings, and bound hands untieing themselves. A later film, Railroad Turnbridge (1976), frames the Willamette River in Portland, Oregon as the bridge turns. Steelmill/Stahwerk (1979), made in collaboration with art historian Clara Weyergraf, is divided into two parts: interviews with German steel factory workers about their work and the forging of Serra's sculpture Berlin Block (for Charlie Chaplin). Survey exhibitions and screenings of his films have been held at the Kunstmuseum Basel, Switzerland in 2017; Anthology Film Archives, New York, October 17–23, 2019; and Harvard Film Archive, January 27 – February 9, 2020. In 2019, Serra donated his entire film and video works to the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan, New York. Serra's first solo exhibition was in 1966 at Galleria Salita in Rome, Italy. His first solo exhibition in the U.S. was at the Leo Castelli Warehouse, New York, in 1969. His first solo museum exhibition was at the Pasadena Art Museum in Pasadena, California in 1970. The first retrospective of his work was held at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986. A second retrospective was held at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 2007. The first survey exhibition of his drawings was at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam in 1977 and traveled to the Kunsthalle Tübingen in 1978. A second retrospective of drawings was presented at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City; the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art; and The Menil Collection, Houston from 2011 to 2012. An overview of Serra's work in film and video was on view at the Kunstmuseum Basel in 2017. Serra enjoyed solo exhibitions at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden in 1978; Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 1980; Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou, Paris, 1983–1984; Museum Haus Lange, Krefeld, in 1985; The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986 and 2007; Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in 1986; Westphalian State Museum of Art and Cultural History, Münster, in 1987; Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus, Munich, in 1987; Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven, in 1988; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, in 1988.

Richard Serra moved to New York City in 1966 and bought a house in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia in 1970, where he spent summers working. He married art historian Clara Weyergraf in 1981. As of 2019, Serra maintained a home in Manhattan and studios in Nova Scotia and on the North Fork of Long Island. His brother is noted San Francisco attorney Tony Serra. Serra enjoyed solo exhibitions at the Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden in 1978; Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 1980; Musée National d'Art Moderne, Centre Pompidou, Paris, from 1983 to 1984; Museum Haus Lange, Krefeld, in 1985; The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1986 and 2007; Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk, in 1986; Westphalian State Museum of Art and Cultural History, Münster, in 1987; Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus, Munich, in 1987; Stedelijk Van Abbemuseum, Eindhoven, in 1988; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, in 1990; Kunsthaus Zürich, in 1990; CAPC Musée d'Art Contemporain, Bordeaux, in 1990; Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, in 1992; Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen, Düsseldorf, in 1992; Dia Center for the Arts, New York, in 1997; Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, from 1998 to 1999; Centro de Arte Hélio Oiticica, Rio de Janeiro, from 1997 to 1998; Trajan's Market, Rome, from 1999 to 2000; Pulitzer Foundation for the Arts, St. Louis, in 2003; National Archaeological Museum, Naples, in 2004; and Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam, in 2017. An overview of his work in film and video was on view at the Kunstmuseum Basel in 2017. Serra's work is included in numerous museums and public collections worldwide, such as The Museum of Modern Art, New York; The Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto; Art Institute of Chicago; Bonnefantenmuseum, Maastricht, The Netherlands; Centre Cultural Fundació La Caixa, Barcelona; Centre Georges Pompidou, Musée National d'Art Moderne, Paris; Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth, Texas; Dia Art Foundation, New York; Guggenheim Museum Bilbao and New York; Pérez Art Museum Miami, Florida; Hamburger Kunsthalle, Hamburg, Germany; Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, DC; Moderna Museet, Stockholm; and Glenstone Museum, Potomac, Maryland. Selected public collections include the City of Bochum, Germany; City of Chicago, Public Art Collection; City of Goslar, Germany; City of Hamburg, Germany; City of St. Louis, Missouri; City of Tokyo, Japan; City of Berlin, Germany; City of Paris, France; and Collection City of Reykjavík, Iceland. Serra received numerous awards, including the Fulbright Grant (1965–66); Guggenheim Fellowship (1970); République Française, Ministère de la Culture et de la Communication Chevalier de l'Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (1985 and 1991); Japan Arts Association, Tokyo Praemium Imperiale (1994); a Leone d'Oro for lifetime achievement at the Venice Biennale, Italy (2001); American Academy of Arts and Letters (2001); Orden pour le Mérite für Wissenschaften und Künste, Federal Republic of Germany (2002); Orden de las Artes y las Letras de España, Spain (2008); The National Arts Award: Lifetime Achievement Award (bestowed by Americans for the Arts in 2014); Hermitage Museum Foundation's Award for Lifetime Contributions to the World of Art (2014); Chevalier de l'Ordre national de la Légion d'honneur, Republic of France (2015); Landesmuseum Wiesbaden Alexej-von-Jawlensky-Preis (2017); and a J. Paul Getty Medal (2018). Serra is also featured as an architect who is a third level Mason in Matthew Barney's film Cremaster 3, part of the five-part Cremaster Cycle. All writings and interviews in the following anthologies are solely by Richard Serra unless otherwise indicated. Richard Serra died from pneumonia at his home in Orient, New York, on March 26, 2024, at the age of 85.
